analysis.one_liner: Protects airline workers from being fired or disciplined for reporting safety violations.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for airlines, their contractors, and Federal Aviation Administration contractors to fire, discipline, or reassign employees who report violations of aviation law, testify in Transportation Department or FAA proceedings, or refuse to break the law on the job. It set up a complaint process at the Department of Labor, with penalties for violators and court review. It also would have barred companies from enforcing secrecy agreements that do not spell out employees' right to report wrongdoing to Congress and federal investigators.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline workers, applicants, and former employees — including FAA and airline contractors and subcontractors — who report safety and legal violations, testify before Congress or in federal proceedings, or refuse to carry out an unlawful instruction. Under the bill, they could file a complaint with the Labor Department within 180 days of being punished, and employers would have to prove by clear and convincing evidence that they would have taken the same action for independent reasons. The flying public would also benefit indirectly, since workers would face less risk for flagging safety problems. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Airline and FAA-contractor employees could not be held liable for starting or participating in Transportation Department or FAA proceedings, for testifying before Congress, or for refusing to violate a law when they reasonably believed the law was being broken. [S2] [S3]

Workers who were discharged, disciplined, or reassigned for these reasons could file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor within 180 days, and the Department could investigate, hold hearings, subpoena witnesses, and impose penalties; courts could also award attorney and expert witness fees. [S2] [S3]

The bill would have barred employers from spending funds to enforce nondisclosure agreements that lack a statement preserving employees' rights to report substantial violations of law to Congress or to Justice Department and agency officials. [S2] [S3]

FAA employees would have gained explicit investigative and enforcement procedures for their existing whistleblower protections, by referencing chapters 12 and 77 of title 5 of the U.S. Code. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and their contractors and subcontractors would bear the cost: complaints at the Department of Labor, the possibility of penalties under the commercial-trucking whistleblower statute the bill borrows, court proceedings, and required rewrites of nondisclosure agreements. The Labor Department would also take on new investigative and hearing work. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The employer escape hatch is narrow but real: even after a worker shows that protected activity was a contributing factor, the employer can avoid all investigation and relief by proving with clear and convincing evidence that it would have taken the same action anyway, meaning many legitimately fired whistleblowers would still lose. [S3]

Airlines and contractors would face new liability and penalty exposure, and with mutual consent cases could go to mediation or arbitration, adding compliance and legal costs that critics of expanded employment liability routinely point to. [S3]

Section 3 reaches beyond airlines: any employer using the federal Standard Forms 312 or 4355 nondisclosure agreements would have had to revise them or stop enforcing them, and the bill carves out looser rules for people connected to intelligence activities, which privacy and security-minded critics could have flagged as an inconsistency. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are meaningful but modest in scope: they cover aviation-sector employees rather than all workers, and the employer's clear-and-convincing defense would have limited how many fired whistleblowers actually win relief. The main cost falls on airlines and their contractors in the form of complaints, penalties, and paperwork, which is the point of a deterrent bill. On balance, a fairly designed, narrowly targeted protection whose main weakness is that it never received any legislative attention at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended, so it never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on July 8, 1998; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. [S1] [S5]
No senator joined as a cosponsor. [S4]
The committee took no further action, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines and their contractors and subcontractors came out ahead: the liability, penalty exposure, and nondisclosure-agreement requirements the bill would have imposed on them never became law.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 8, 1998; it was read twice and referred to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (Chair John McCain)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: 0 of 100 senators
against.what_they_did: Not one senator cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors, so there is no record of how either party would have lined up; the only recorded action was a Republican sponsor's referral to a Republican-run committee that did nothing.

industries.note: The bill would have made airlines liable for discriminating against employees who report violations, testify, or refuse to break the law, with Labor Department complaints, penalties, and possible fee awards. Airlines' interest in avoiding that liability ran against the safety-reporting interests of their workers and passengers.

industries.industry: Airline and FAA contractors and subcontractors
industries.note: The bill expressly covered contractors and subcontractors of the FAA and of air carriers, exposing them to the same discrimination prohibition and Labor Department procedures.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and employers using government nondisclosure forms
industries.note: Section 3 would have barred spending funds to enforce Standard Forms 312 and 4355 or any secrecy agreement lacking a statement that whistleblowing to Congress and investigators remains protected, forcing revisions to those agreements.
